err != nil {\n\t\tpanic(err)\n\t}\n}\n\n```\n\nExpected behaviour:\n```console\n$ go run . __complete x\n[Debug] [Error] __complete, x\n:0\nCompletion ended with directive: ShellCompDirectiveDefault\n```\n\nActual behaviour:\n```console\n$ go run . __complete x\n[Debug] [Error] __complete, --\n:0\nCompletion ended with directive: ShellCompDirectiveDefault\n```', 'state': 'CLOSED', 'user': {'login': 'jonathan-conder'}, 'assignees': [], 'comments': 2, 'created_at': '2025-03-12T00:29:59Z', 'updated_at': '2026-04-24T20:41:59Z'}, {'number': 2254, 'title': 'How do you add a shorthand to an option?', 'body': 'You would like to add a shorthand to an option.\n\nHow would you add a shorthand to an option (e.g., `f` in `--flag`)?', 'state': 'CLOSED', 'user': {'login': 'switchupcb'}, 'assignees': [], 'comments': 1, 'created_at': '2025-03-07T01:01:09Z', 'updated_at': '2025-03-07T01:06:42Z'}, {'number': 2252, 'title': 'How do you place help at the top?', 'body': 'You would like to place `help` command at the top of the `Available Commands` list.\n\n```\nAvailable Commands:\n  ex         short description of ex\n  help        Help about any command\n  yz short description of yz\n```\n\nHow do you place help at the top of the available commands list?', 'state': 'CLOSED', 'user': {'login': 'switchupcb'}, 'assignees': [], 'comments': 1, 'created_at': '2025-03-06T16:49:01Z', 'updated_at': '2025-03-07T00:57:34Z'}, {'number': 2250, 'title': 'How do you use one - instead of two -- ?', 'body': "You would like to use one dash (e.g., `-flag`) for a flag, rather than two (e.g., `--flag`).\n\nHow do you use one `-` instead of two `--`?\n\nOtherwise, you receive `Error: unknown shorthand flag: 'f' in -flag`.", 'state': 'CLOSED', 'user': {'login': 'switchupcb'}, 'assignees': [], 'comments': 1, 'created_at': '2025-03-06T15:59:49Z', 'updated_at': '2025-03-07T00:58:02Z'}, {'number': 2247, 'title': 'Running root command with subcommands enabled', 'body': 'I have a CLI app that is pretty simple. As expected, I can also run the sub-command when it\'s attached.  \n\nThe issue comes about when the sub-command is attached to root, and I just try to run `./myapp -a key value`. \n\nI get `Error: unkown command` \n\nI found this issue on the github closely resembling my problem and you\'ll see in my minimum reproduction code I try to do something similar to the answer.  Although I\'ll admit I don\'t 100% understand what the responder is getting at for the fix. \n\n```\nfunc TestRepro(t *testing.T) {\n\tos.Args = make([]string, 0)\n\t// ! Works and executes sub command\n\tos.Args = append(os.Args, []string{"app", "sub"}...)\n\tminRepro()\n\n\t// Does not work, error "Error: unknown command "RunRootCommand" for "app""\n\tos.Args = make([]string, 0)\n\tos.Args = append(os.Args, []string{"app", "RunRootCommand"}...)\n\tminRepro()\n}\n\nfunc minRepro() {\n\t// Define the root command\n\t// fmt.Printf("Args...%v", os.Args)\n\tvar rootCmd = &cobra.Command{\n\t\tUse:   "app",\n\t\tShort: "Root command with catch-all behavior",\n\t\tLong:  "This is the root command of the CLI application with a catch-all feature.",\n\t\tRun: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {\n\n\t\t\t// cobra.ArbitraryArgs(cmd, []string{"TestThisArgs"})\n\n\t\t\tif len(args) > 0 {\n\t\t\t\tfmt.Println("Executing here..")\n\t\t\t} else {\n\t\t\t\tfmt.Println("Root command executed!")\n\t\t\t}\n\t\t},\n\t}\n\n\t// Define a subcommand\n\tvar subCmd = &cobra.Command{\n\t\tUse:   "sub",\n\t\tShort: "Subcommand that does something specific",\n\t\tLong:  "This is a subcommand of the root command.",\n\t\tRun: func(cmd *cobra.Command, args []string) {\n\t\t\tfmt.Println("Subcommand executed!")\n\t\t},\n\t}\n\n\t// Add the subcommand to the root command\n\trootCmd.AddCommand(subCmd)\n\n\t// Override default behavior for unknown commands\n\trootCmd.SetHelpCommand(&cobra.Command{Hidden: true}) // Hide default help command\n\trootCmd.SetFlagErrorFunc(func(cmd *cobra.Command, err error) error {\n\t\tfmt.Printf("Unknown flag or argument: %s\\n", err)\n\t\treturn nil\n\t})\n\n\t// Check if we\'re just running root command.  Basically if "sub" is not in args,\n\t// Forward to root command\n\t// ! From the github issue?\n\tfound := false\n\tfor _, a := range os.Args {\n\t\tif a == "sub" {\n\t\t\tfound = true\n\t\t\tbreak\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tif !found {\n\t\tos.Args = append([]string{"app"}, os.Args...)\n\t}\n\n\tif err := rootCmd.Execute(); err != nil {\n\t\tfmt.Println(err)\n\t\tos.Exit(1)\n\t}\n}\n```\n\nThe code at the bottom of `minRepro()` was just a stab at this github issue: [https://github.com/spf13/cobra/issues/2162](url). \n\nIt seems like a hack and so I\'m not confident that\'s even close to the implementation I need here to resolve this. {'number': 2547, 'title': 'Docs: contributor architecture overview for the `cobra` package', 'body': "The package is flat (all in the repo root), so it isn't obvious where things live. I drafted a short page (proposed `site/content/architecture.md`, draft below) mapping the files and the `Execute()` flow. Would you take it as a PR? Happy to close if not.\n\nDisclosure: I maintain RepoLens, a docs tool, and used it (v1.15.2) for the first draft; everything was checked against the source by hand.\n\n<details><summary>Draft site/content/architecture.md</summary>\n\n# Architecture (for contributors)\n\nAll of Cobra is one Go package in the repo root; `doc/` is a separate package that generates man/markdown/rst/yaml docs. Dependencies: `spf13/pflag` (flags), `inconshreveable/mousetrap` (Windows Explorer detection) and `cpuguy83/go-md2man` (for `doc/`).\n\n| File | What it holds |\n|---|---|\n| `command.go` (~2,100 lines) | `Command`: tree building, `Execute`/`ExecuteC`, `Find`/`Traverse`, flag parsing, hooks, help/usage/version. |\n| `cobra.go` | Package globals and template functions, `OnInitialize`, `EnableCommandSorting`, etc. |\n| `args.go` | Positional-arg validators (`NoArgs`, `ExactArgs`, `MatchAll`, …). |\n| `flag_groups.go` | `MarkFlagsRequiredTogether`, `MarkFlagsMutuallyExclusive`, `MarkFlagsOneRequired`. |\n| `completions.go` (~1,000) | The hidden `__complete` command, `ValidArgsFunction`, and the default `completion` command. |\n| `bash_completions*.go`, `zsh_`, `fish_`, `powershell_completions.go` | Shell-specific completion script generators. |\n| `active_help.go` | Active Help messages shown during completion. |\n| `command_win.go` / `command_notwin.go` | Platform-specific pre-exec (mousetrap). |\n\n## How `Execute()` runs\n1. `Execute()` calls `ExecuteC()` on the root, which adds the default help and completion commands (`InitDefaultHelpCmd`, `InitDefaultCompletionCmd`).\n2. It finds the target with `Find(args)` (or `Traverse` when `TraverseChildren` is set).\n3. `execute()` parses flags, handles `--help`/`--version`, validates args and flag groups, then runs `PersistentPreRun` → `PreRun` → `Run` → `PostRun` → `PersistentPostRun` (the `E` variants return errors).\n\n---\n<sub>Drafted with [RepoLens](https://github.com/CHAPIBUNNY/repolens), checked by hand.</sub>\n\n</details>\n", 'state': 'open', 'html_url': 'https://github.com/spf13/cobra/issues/2547', 'user': {'login': 'CHAPIBUNNY', 'id': 162579999, 'profile_url': 'https://github.com/CHAPIBUNNY', 'avatar_url': 'https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/162579999?v=4'}, 'author_association': 'NONE', 'assignees': [], 'comments': 1, 'reactions': {'total_count': 0, '+1': 0, '-1': 0, 'laugh': 0, 'confused': 0, 'heart': 0, 'hooray': 0, 'rocket': 0, 'eyes': 0}, 'created_at': '2026-10-21T18:55:13Z', 'updated_at': '2026-10-24T08:34:14Z', 'has_parent': False, 'has_children': False, 'closed_by_pull_requests': {'total_count': 0, 'references': []}}

The next positional is consumed as that flag\'s "value" and the following positional happens to match a subcommand — so the child handler runs, the first post-`--` positional is silently dropped, and the parent\'s positionals never reach any command.\n\nReproduction from the issue:\n\n```go\nroot := &cobra.Command{Use:"app", TraverseChildren:true, Args:cobra.ArbitraryArgs,\n    Run: func(_ *cobra.Command, args []string){ fmt.Printf("root called with %q\\\\n", args) }}\nroot.AddCommand(&cobra.Command{Use:"child",\n    Run: func(*cobra.Command, []string){ fmt.Println("child called") }})\nroot.Execute()\n```\n\n```\n$ ./app -- literal child\nchild called                 # bug: wrong handler, "literal" lost\n$ # expected:\nroot called with ["literal" "child"]\n```\n\nThe default (non-traverse) `stripFlags` path already stops command discovery on `--`.\n\n## Fix\n\nMirror that behaviour. 2510, 'state': 'open', 'locked': False, 'title': "Handle combined shorthands in Traverse's value-flag detection", 'body': '## `Traverse` mishandles a combined shorthand cluster that ends in a value flag\n\n### Description\n\n`command.go`, in `Traverse`, the "short flag with a space separated value" case:\n\n```go\ncase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") && len(arg) == 2 && !shortHasNoOptDefVal(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n    inFlag = true\n```\n\n`len(arg) == 2` recognises only a **single** shorthand. A combined cluster such as `-ab` (where `-a` is a bool and `-b` takes a value) is mis-handled: `Traverse` appends `-ab` to `flags` **without** setting `inFlag`, so the following argument is looked up as a **subcommand name**.\n\n### Why it\'s wrong\n\npflag\'s real rule — verified directly with `pflag parse [-ab sub2] err=<nil> args=[] all=true bind="sub2"` — is that the first shorthand lacking a `NoOptDefVal` swallows the rest of the cluster, and only reaches into the next argv slot when it is the *last* shorthand. Cobra must predict that split in order to locate the target command, and for clusters it predicts wrong.\n\nWith `TraverseChildren: true`, `prog child -ab grandchild` fails with:\n\n```\nflag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n```\n\neven though the value *was* supplied — and the equivalent `prog child -a -b grandchild` works. Valid input is rejected with a misleading error.\n\n### Upstream status\n\n- Issue **#2188** ("Combining shorthand flags before command names does not work") is open but is about flags *before* the command name (`mycli -C elephant first second`).\n- PR **#2189** ("Fix shorthand combination edge case") is open and unmerged, and its diff touches only `stripFlags` / `argsMinusFirstX` / `Find` — it does **not** touch `Traverse`, so the `TraverseChildren: true` path is unfixed by any open PR.\n\n## The fix\n\n```go\n// shortCombinationTakesNextArg reports whether the value of a single dash\n// shorthand argument (such as "-a" or "-ab") is taken from the following\n// argument, rather than being embedded in the argument itself.\n//\n// This mirrors how pflag parses shorthand arguments: the first shorthand of the\n// combination that does not have a NoOptDefVal consumes the remainder of the\n// combination as its value, and it only reaches out to the next argument when\n// that shorthand is the last one of the combination. So "-ab value" consumes\n// "value" for -b (when -a is a boolean), while "-bvalue" does not.\nfunc shortCombinationTakesNextArg(combination string, fs *flag.FlagSet) bool {\n\tlast := len(combination) - 1\n\tfor i := 0; i <= last; i++ {\n\t\tif !shortHasNoOptDefVal(combination[i:i+1], fs) {\n\t\t\t// This shorthand needs a value. It only comes from the next argument\n\t\t\t// if the combination ends here.\n\t\t\treturn i == last\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn false\n}\n```\n\nand in `Traverse`:\n\n```diff\n-\t\tcase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") && len(arg) == 2 && !shortHasNoOptDefVal(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n+\t\tcase len(arg) > 1 && strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") &&\n+\t\t\tshortCombinationTakesNextArg(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n```\n\nThe `len(arg) > 1` guard is load-bearing: without it a bare `-` (which pflag treats as a positional argument) would start matching and get appended to `flags`.\n\n## Tests\n\n`TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue` (6 subtests) and `TestExecuteCombinedShorthandWithValue`, both added to `command_test.go`.\n\n- Before:\n  ```\n  --- FAIL: TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue/cluster_ending_in_a_value_flag\n      command_test.go:2501: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n  --- FAIL: TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue/cluster_ending_in_an_inherited_value_flag\n      command_test.go:2501: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'C\' in -C\n  --- FAIL: TestExecuteCombinedShorthandWithValue\n      command_test.go:2543: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n  ```\n  After: all pass.\n- Four control subtests (`value_inside_the_cluster`, `all_boolean_cluster`, `single_value_flag`, `single_bool_flag`) pass **both** before and after, proving the fix does not over-consume arguments.\n- `go test ./...`: root package **404 → 412 PASS** (+8), `cobra/doc` 19 PASS, **0 failures**. Baseline on unmodified HEAD was fully green with zero pre-existing failures. `go vet ./...` clean.\n\nThe 36 `gofmt -l` hits are a pre-existing repo-wide CRLF artefact of this Windows checkout — identical count before and after, so this change adds none.\n\n## Note\n\nThis repository asks contributors to sign a CLA; I have not done so, since that is a legal attestation only the contributor can make.\n', 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'januththedev', 'id': 96273863, 'user_view_type': 'public', 'node_id': 'U_kgDOBb0Fxw', 'avatar_url': 'state': 'open', 'locked': False, 'title': 'Provide usefull errors when using invalid sub command', 'body': "If the *TraverseChildren* mode is active, the *Traverse* function returns the last accepted command along the requested sub command chain. This command is then used to parse the arguments. This will for sure fail, if the traversing was aborted because an invalid sub command was given. As a result, cobra complains about invalid flags instead of an invalid sub command.\r\n\r\nThis behaviour might be useful, if the intermediate command is *Runnable()*, but it for sure makes no sense, if it isn't.\r\n\r\nThis PR fixes this by providing a *legacyArgs()* error in case of not runnable intermediate commands.\r\n\r\n---\r\n*Remark:* It solves the obvious problematic behaviour, but basically the general scenario is more complex.\r\nIf the intermediate command is *Runnable()* in addition to providing additional sub commands, then it should be possible to forward the control about the error message to the command to be a able to distinguish between these two cases according to its needs. This is basically already possible by declaring a *FlagErrorFunc()*. But unfortunately it only gets the command and error as arguments, but not the actual set of arguments. Therefore it has no chance to detect the actual problem and provide appropriate error feedback.\r\n\r\nSolving this is more invasive, because it would require, either to change the interface, or add another more general error handler option.\r\n\r\n", 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'mandelsoft', 'id': 553075, 'user_view_type': 'public', 'node_id': 'MDQ6VXNlcjU1MzA3NQ==', 'title': 'fix: treat lone dash as positional during command discovery', 'body': 'When a runnable root command accepts positional arguments and has a `child` subcommand, `root - child` currently executes `child` with `-` as its argument. Replacing `-` with an ordinary filename keeps execution on the root. Enabling `TraverseChildren` also keeps the lone dash on the root, consistent with pflag treating `-` as a positional argument.\n\nUse the existing `isFlagArg` predicate in command discovery and matched-command removal. A lone dash can then stop subcommand discovery like other positional arguments. If an application explicitly defines `-` as a command name or alias, its command token is removed normally. Flag values and the `--` terminator retain their existing handling.\n\nValidation on macOS arm64 with Go 1.25.3:\n\n- The strip-flags case and default-dispatch regressions failed before the fix.\n- Added coverage for lone dashes before and after a subcommand, after a boolean flag, as a flag value, around `--`, and as a command name or alias.\n- `go test ./...` passes.\n- `make all` (formatting and full tests) and `git diff --check` pass. The optional golangci-lint binary is not installed locally.\n\nAI assistance: OpenAI Codex helped implement and test this change.\n', 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'ibrahimypr', 'state': 'closed', 'locked': False, 'title': 'fix: prevent completions from mutating os.Args via append side effect', 'body': '## Summary\n\n- Fixes a bug where `getCompletions()` accidentally mutates `os.Args` by writing `"--"` into the shared backing array via an `append` with spare capacity\n- Uses a three-index slice expression (`finalArgs[:len:len]`) to cap the slice capacity, forcing `append` to allocate a new array\n- Adds a regression test that confirms the args slice is not corrupted during shell completion\n\n## Details\n\nWhen shell completions are requested (e.g., `prog __complete x`), `getCompletions()` calls:\n\n```go\n_ = finalCmd.ParseFlags(append(finalArgs, "--"))\n```\n\n`finalArgs` is a sub-slice of the original args (derived from `os.Args[1:]`), and if it has spare capacity in its backing array, `append` writes `"--"` directly into the shared memory rather than allocating a new slice. This corrupts `os.Args`, which users may be inspecting in their `ValidArgsFunction`.\n\nThe fix uses `finalArgs[:len(finalArgs):len(finalArgs)]` to limit the capacity to the length, guaranteeing that `append` allocates a fresh backing array.\n\nThe bug is most visible with `TraverseChildren: true`, since `Traverse()` returns sub-slices that preserve the original backing array\'s capacity.\n\nFixes #2257\n\n## Test plan\n\n- [x] Added `TestCompletionDoesNotMutateArgs` that fails without the fix and passes with it\n- [x] Full test suite passes (`go test ./...`)', 'author_association': 'title': "command: stop Traverse at `--` so a positional isn't run as a subcommand", 'body': '## Bug (fixes #2528)\n\nWith `TraverseChildren: true`, the long-flag branch of `Command.Traverse` matched a bare `--` as a flag that "takes a value":\n\n```go\ncase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "--") && !strings.Contains(arg, "="):\n    inFlag = !hasNoOptDefVal(arg[2:], c.Flags())\n    flags = append(flags, arg)\n    continue\n```\n\n`arg[2:]` is `""`, no flag by that name exists, so `inFlag = true`. The next positional is consumed as that flag\'s "value" and the following positional happens to match a subcommand — so the child handler runs, the first post-`--` positional is silently dropped, and the parent\'s positionals never reach any command.\n\nReproduction from the issue:\n\n```go\nroot := &cobra.Command{Use:"app", TraverseChildren:true, Args:cobra.ArbitraryArgs,\n    Run: func(_ *cobra.Command, args []string){ fmt.Printf("root called with %q\\\\n", args) }}\nroot.AddCommand(&cobra.Command{Use:"child",\n    Run: func(*cobra.Command, []string){ fmt.Println("child called") }})\nroot.Execute()\n```\n\n```\n$ ./app -- literal child\nchild called                 # bug: wrong handler, "literal" lost\n$ # expected:\nroot called with ["literal" "child"]\n```\n\nThe default (non-traverse) `stripFlags` path already stops command discovery on `--`.\n\n## Fix\n\nMirror that behaviour. When `Traverse` sees a bare `--`:\n\n1. Parse any flags accumulated so far on the current command.\n2. Return the current command along with the remaining args starting at the delimiter, so a downstream parser sees the exact slice it would have gotten without `TraverseChildren`.\n\n## Test\n\n`TestTraverseStopsAtEndOfFlags` covers two cases:\n\n- `[]string{"--", "literal", "child"}` → traversal stays on root, remaining is unchanged.\n- `[]string{"--", "child"}` → traversal stays on 2510, 'state': 'open', 'locked': False, 'title': "Handle combined shorthands in Traverse's value-flag detection", 'body': '## `Traverse` mishandles a combined shorthand cluster that ends in a value flag\n\n### Description\n\n`command.go`, in `Traverse`, the "short flag with a space separated value" case:\n\n```go\ncase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") && len(arg) == 2 && !shortHasNoOptDefVal(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n    inFlag = true\n```\n\n`len(arg) == 2` recognises only a **single** shorthand. A combined cluster such as `-ab` (where `-a` is a bool and `-b` takes a value) is mis-handled: `Traverse` appends `-ab` to `flags` **without** setting `inFlag`, so the following argument is looked up as a **subcommand name**.\n\n### Why it\'s wrong\n\npflag\'s real rule — verified directly with `pflag parse [-ab sub2] err=<nil> args=[] all=true bind="sub2"` — is that the first shorthand lacking a `NoOptDefVal` swallows the rest of the cluster, and only reaches into the next argv slot when it is the *last* shorthand. Cobra must predict that split in order to locate the target command, and for clusters it predicts wrong.\n\nWith `TraverseChildren: true`, `prog child -ab grandchild` fails with:\n\n```\nflag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n```\n\neven though the value *was* supplied — and the equivalent `prog child -a -b grandchild` works. Valid input is rejected with a misleading error.\n\n### Upstream status\n\n- Issue **#2188** ("Combining shorthand flags before command names does not work") is open but is about flags *before* the command name (`mycli -C elephant first second`).\n- PR **#2189** ("Fix shorthand combination edge case") is open and unmerged, and its diff touches only `stripFlags` / `argsMinusFirstX` / `Find` — it does **not** touch `Traverse`, so the `TraverseChildren: true` path is unfixed by any open PR.\n\n## The fix\n\n```go\n// shortCombinationTakesNextArg reports whether the value of a single dash\n// shorthand argument (such as "-a" or "-ab") is taken from the following\n// argument, rather than being embedded in the argument itself.\n//\n// This mirrors how pflag parses shorthand arguments: the first shorthand of the\n// combination that does not have a NoOptDefVal consumes the remainder of the\n// combination as its value, and it only reaches out to the next argument when\n// that shorthand is the last one of the combination. So "-ab value" consumes\n// "value" for -b (when -a is a boolean), while "-bvalue" does not.\nfunc shortCombinationTakesNextArg(combination string, fs *flag.FlagSet) bool {\n\tlast := len(combination) - 1\n\tfor i := 0; i <= last; i++ {\n\t\tif !shortHasNoOptDefVal(combination[i:i+1], fs) {\n\t\t\t// This shorthand needs a value. It only comes from the next argument\n\t\t\t// if the combination ends here.\n\t\t\treturn i == last\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn false\n}\n```\n\nand in `Traverse`:\n\n```diff\n-\t\tcase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") && len(arg) == 2 && !shortHasNoOptDefVal(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n+\t\tcase len(arg) > 1 && strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") &&\n+\t\t\tshortCombinationTakesNextArg(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n```\n\nThe `len(arg) > 1` guard is load-bearing: without it a bare `-` (which pflag treats as a positional argument) would start matching and get appended to `flags`.\n\n## Tests\n\n`TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue` (6 subtests) and `TestExecuteCombinedShorthandWithValue`, both added to `command_test.go`.\n\n- Before:\n  ```\n  --- FAIL: TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue/cluster_ending_in_a_value_flag\n      command_test.go:2501: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n  --- FAIL: TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue/cluster_ending_in_an_inherited_value_flag\n      command_test.go:2501: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'C\' in -C\n  --- FAIL: TestExecuteCombinedShorthandWithValue\n      command_test.go:2543: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n  ```\n  After: all pass.\n- Four control subtests (`value_inside_the_cluster`, `all_boolean_cluster`, `single_value_flag`, `single_bool_flag`) pass **both** before and after, proving the fix does not over-consume arguments.\n- `go test ./...`: root package **404 → 412 PASS** (+8), `cobra/doc` 19 PASS, **0 failures**. Baseline on unmodified HEAD was fully green with zero pre-existing failures. `go vet ./...` clean.\n\nThe 36 `gofmt -l` hits are a pre-existing repo-wide CRLF artefact of this Windows checkout — identical count before and after, so this change adds none.\n\n## Note\n\nThis repository asks contributors to sign a CLA; I have not done so, since that is a legal attestation only the contributor can make.\n', 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'januththedev', 'id': 96273863, 'user_view_type': 'public', 'node_id': 'U_kgDOBb0Fxw', 'avatar_url': 'state': 'open', 'locked': False, 'title': 'Provide usefull errors when using invalid sub command', 'body': "If the *TraverseChildren* mode is active, the *Traverse* function returns the last accepted command along the requested sub command chain. This command is then used to parse the arguments. This will for sure fail, if the traversing was aborted because an invalid sub command was given. As a result, cobra complains about invalid flags instead of an invalid sub command.\r\n\r\nThis behaviour might be useful, if the intermediate command is *Runnable()*, but it for sure makes no sense, if it isn't.\r\n\r\nThis PR fixes this by providing a *legacyArgs()* error in case of not runnable intermediate commands.\r\n\r\n---\r\n*Remark:* It solves the obvious problematic behaviour, but basically the general scenario is more complex.\r\nIf the intermediate command is *Runnable()* in addition to providing additional sub commands, then it should be possible to forward the control about the error message to the command to be a able to distinguish between these two cases according to its needs. This is basically already possible by declaring a *FlagErrorFunc()*. But unfortunately it only gets the command and error as arguments, but not the actual set of arguments. Therefore it has no chance to detect the actual problem and provide appropriate error feedback.\r\n\r\nSolving this is more invasive, because it would require, either to change the interface, or add another more general error handler option.\r\n\r\n", 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'mandelsoft', 'id': 553075, 'user_view_type': 'public', 'node_id': 'MDQ6VXNlcjU1MzA3NQ==', 'title': 'fix: treat lone dash as positional during command discovery', 'body': 'When a runnable root command accepts positional arguments and has a `child` subcommand, `root - child` currently executes `child` with `-` as its argument. Replacing `-` with an ordinary filename keeps execution on the root. Enabling `TraverseChildren` also keeps the lone dash on the root, consistent with pflag treating `-` as a positional argument.\n\nUse the existing `isFlagArg` predicate in command discovery and matched-command removal. A lone dash can then stop subcommand discovery like other positional arguments. If an application explicitly defines `-` as a command name or alias, its command token is removed normally. Flag values and the `--` terminator retain their existing handling.\n\nValidation on macOS arm64 with Go 1.25.3:\n\n- The strip-flags case and default-dispatch regressions failed before the fix.\n- Added coverage for lone dashes before and after a subcommand, after a boolean flag, as a flag value, around `--`, and as a command name or alias.\n- `go test ./...` passes.\n- `make all` (formatting and full tests) and `git diff --check` pass. The optional golangci-lint binary is not installed locally.\n\nAI assistance: OpenAI Codex helped implement and test this change.\n', 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'ibrahimypr', 'state': 'closed', 'locked': False, 'title': 'fix: prevent completions from mutating os.Args via append side effect', 'body': '## Summary\n\n- Fixes a bug where `getCompletions()` accidentally mutates `os.Args` by writing `"--"` into the shared backing array via an `append` with spare capacity\n- Uses a three-index slice expression (`finalArgs[:len:len]`) to cap the slice capacity, forcing `append` to allocate a new array\n- Adds a regression test that confirms the args slice is not corrupted during shell completion\n\n## Details\n\nWhen shell completions are requested (e.g., `prog __complete x`), `getCompletions()` calls:\n\n```go\n_ = finalCmd.ParseFlags(append(finalArgs, "--"))\n```\n\n`finalArgs` is a sub-slice of the original args (derived from `os.Args[1:]`), and if it has spare capacity in its backing array, `append` writes `"--"` directly into the shared memory rather than allocating a new slice. This corrupts `os.Args`, which users may be inspecting in their `ValidArgsFunction`.\n\nThe fix uses `finalArgs[:len(finalArgs):len(finalArgs)]` to limit the capacity to the length, guaranteeing that `append` allocates a fresh backing array.\n\nThe bug is most visible with `TraverseChildren: true`, since `Traverse()` returns sub-slices that preserve the original backing array\'s capacity.\n\nFixes #2257\n\n## Test plan\n\n- [x] Added `TestCompletionDoesNotMutateArgs` that fails without the fix and passes with it\n- [x] Full test suite passes (`go test ./...`)', 'author_association': 'title': "command: stop Traverse at `--` so a positional isn't run as a subcommand", 'body': '## Bug (fixes #2528)\n\nWith `TraverseChildren: true`, the long-flag branch of `Command.Traverse` matched a bare `--` as a flag that "takes a value":\n\n```go\ncase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "--") && !strings.Contains(arg, "="):\n    inFlag = !hasNoOptDefVal(arg[2:], c.Flags())\n    flags = append(flags, arg)\n    continue\n```\n\n`arg[2:]` is `""`, no flag by that name exists, so `inFlag = true`. The next positional is consumed as that flag\'s "value" and the following positional happens to match a subcommand — so the child handler runs, the first post-`--` positional is silently dropped, and the parent\'s positionals never reach any command.\n\nReproduction from the issue:\n\n```go\nroot := &cobra.Command{Use:"app", TraverseChildren:true, Args:cobra.ArbitraryArgs,\n    Run: func(_ *cobra.Command, args []string){ fmt.Printf("root called with %q\\\\n", args) }}\nroot.AddCommand(&cobra.Command{Use:"child",\n    Run: func(*cobra.Command, []string){ fmt.Println("child called") }})\nroot.Execute()\n```\n\n```\n$ ./app -- literal child\nchild called                 # bug: wrong handler, "literal" lost\n$ # expected:\nroot called with ["literal" "child"]\n```\n\nThe default (non-traverse) `stripFlags` path already stops command discovery on `--`.\n\n## Fix\n\nMirror that behaviour. When `Traverse` sees a bare `--`:\n\n1. Parse any flags accumulated so far on the current command.\n2. Return the current command along with the remaining args starting at the delimiter, so a downstream parser sees the exact slice it would have gotten without `TraverseChildren`.\n\n## Test\n\n`TestTraverseStopsAtEndOfFlags` covers two cases:\n\n- `[]string{"--", "literal", "child"}` → traversal stays on root, remaining is unchanged.\n- `[]string{"--", "child"}` → traversal stays on 2510, 'state': 'open', 'locked': False, 'title': "Handle combined shorthands in Traverse's value-flag detection", 'body': '## `Traverse` mishandles a combined shorthand cluster that ends in a value flag\n\n### Description\n\n`command.go`, in `Traverse`, the "short flag with a space separated value" case:\n\n```go\ncase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") && len(arg) == 2 && !shortHasNoOptDefVal(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n    inFlag = true\n```\n\n`len(arg) == 2` recognises only a **single** shorthand. A combined cluster such as `-ab` (where `-a` is a bool and `-b` takes a value) is mis-handled: `Traverse` appends `-ab` to `flags` **without** setting `inFlag`, so the following argument is looked up as a **subcommand name**.\n\n### Why it\'s wrong\n\npflag\'s real rule — verified directly with `pflag parse [-ab sub2] err=<nil> args=[] all=true bind="sub2"` — is that the first shorthand lacking a `NoOptDefVal` swallows the rest of the cluster, and only reaches into the next argv slot when it is the *last* shorthand. Cobra must predict that split in order to locate the target command, and for clusters it predicts wrong.\n\nWith `TraverseChildren: true`, `prog child -ab grandchild` fails with:\n\n```\nflag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n```\n\neven though the value *was* supplied — and the equivalent `prog child -a -b grandchild` works. Valid input is rejected with a misleading error.\n\n### Upstream status\n\n- Issue **#2188** ("Combining shorthand flags before command names does not work") is open but is about flags *before* the command name (`mycli -C elephant first second`).\n- PR **#2189** ("Fix shorthand combination edge case") is open and unmerged, and its diff touches only `stripFlags` / `argsMinusFirstX` / `Find` — it does **not** touch `Traverse`, so the `TraverseChildren: true` path is unfixed by any open PR.\n\n## The fix\n\n```go\n// shortCombinationTakesNextArg reports whether the value of a single dash\n// shorthand argument (such as "-a" or "-ab") is taken from the following\n// argument, rather than being embedded in the argument itself.\n//\n// This mirrors how pflag parses shorthand arguments: the first shorthand of the\n// combination that does not have a NoOptDefVal consumes the remainder of the\n// combination as its value, and it only reaches out to the next argument when\n// that shorthand is the last one of the combination. So "-ab value" consumes\n// "value" for -b (when -a is a boolean), while "-bvalue" does not.\nfunc shortCombinationTakesNextArg(combination string, fs *flag.FlagSet) bool {\n\tlast := len(combination) - 1\n\tfor i := 0; i <= last; i++ {\n\t\tif !shortHasNoOptDefVal(combination[i:i+1], fs) {\n\t\t\t// This shorthand needs a value. It only comes from the next argument\n\t\t\t// if the combination ends here.\n\t\t\treturn i == last\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn false\n}\n```\n\nand in `Traverse`:\n\n```diff\n-\t\tcase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") && len(arg) == 2 && !shortHasNoOptDefVal(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n+\t\tcase len(arg) > 1 && strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") &&\n+\t\t\tshortCombinationTakesNextArg(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n```\n\nThe `len(arg) > 1` guard is load-bearing: without it a bare `-` (which pflag treats as a positional argument) would start matching and get appended to `flags`.\n\n## Tests\n\n`TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue` (6 subtests) and `TestExecuteCombinedShorthandWithValue`, both added to `command_test.go`.\n\n- Before:\n  ```\n  --- FAIL: TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue/cluster_ending_in_a_value_flag\n      command_test.go:2501: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n  --- FAIL: TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue/cluster_ending_in_an_inherited_value_flag\n      command_test.go:2501: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'C\' in -C\n  --- FAIL: TestExecuteCombinedShorthandWithValue\n      command_test.go:2543: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n  ```\n  After: all pass.\n- Four control subtests (`value_inside_the_cluster`, `all_boolean_cluster`, `single_value_flag`, `single_bool_flag`) pass **both** before and after, proving the fix does not over-consume arguments.\n- `go test ./...`: root package **404 → 412 PASS** (+8), `cobra/doc` 19 PASS, **0 failures**. Baseline on unmodified HEAD was fully green with zero pre-existing failures. `go vet ./...` clean.\n\nThe 36 `gofmt -l` hits are a pre-existing repo-wide CRLF artefact of this Windows checkout — identical count before and after, so this change adds none.\n\n## Note\n\nThis repository asks contributors to sign a CLA; I have not done so, since that is a legal attestation only the contributor can make.\n', 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'januththedev', 'id': 96273863, 'user_view_type': 'public', 'node_id': 'U_kgDOBb0Fxw', 'avatar_url': 'state': 'open', 'locked': False, 'title': 'Provide usefull errors when using invalid sub command', 'body': "If the *TraverseChildren* mode is active, the *Traverse* function returns the last accepted command along the requested sub command chain. This command is then used to parse the arguments. This will for sure fail, if the traversing was aborted because an invalid sub command was given. As a result, cobra complains about invalid flags instead of an invalid sub command.\r\n\r\nThis behaviour might be useful, if the intermediate command is *Runnable()*, but it for sure makes no sense, if it isn't.\r\n\r\nThis PR fixes this by providing a *legacyArgs()* error in case of not runnable intermediate commands.\r\n\r\n---\r\n*Remark:* It solves the obvious problematic behaviour, but basically the general scenario is more complex.\r\nIf the intermediate command is *Runnable()* in addition to providing additional sub commands, then it should be possible to forward the control about the error message to the command to be a able to distinguish between these two cases according to its needs. This is basically already possible by declaring a *FlagErrorFunc()*. But unfortunately it only gets the command and error as arguments, but not the actual set of arguments. Therefore it has no chance to detect the actual problem and provide appropriate error feedback.\r\n\r\nSolving this is more invasive, because it would require, either to change the interface, or add another more general error handler option.\r\n\r\n", 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'mandelsoft', 'id': 553075, 'user_view_type': 'public', 'node_id': 'MDQ6VXNlcjU1MzA3NQ==', 'title': 'fix: treat lone dash as positional during command discovery', 'body': 'When a runnable root command accepts positional arguments and has a `child` subcommand, `root - child` currently executes `child` with `-` as its argument. Replacing `-` with an ordinary filename keeps execution on the root. Enabling `TraverseChildren` also keeps the lone dash on the root, consistent with pflag treating `-` as a positional argument.\n\nUse the existing `isFlagArg` predicate in command discovery and matched-command removal. A lone dash can then stop subcommand discovery like other positional arguments. If an application explicitly defines `-` as a command name or alias, its command token is removed normally. Flag values and the `--` terminator retain their existing handling.\n\nValidation on macOS arm64 with Go 1.25.3:\n\n- The strip-flags case and default-dispatch regressions failed before the fix.\n- Added coverage for lone dashes before and after a subcommand, after a boolean flag, as a flag value, around `--`, and as a command name or alias.\n- `go test ./...` passes.\n- `make all` (formatting and full tests) and `git diff --check` pass. The optional golangci-lint binary is not installed locally.\n\nAI assistance: OpenAI Codex helped implement and test this change.\n', 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'ibrahimypr', 'state': 'closed', 'locked': False, 'title': 'fix: prevent completions from mutating os.Args via append side effect', 'body': '## Summary\n\n- Fixes a bug where `getCompletions()` accidentally mutates `os.Args` by writing `"--"` into the shared backing array via an `append` with spare capacity\n- Uses a three-index slice expression (`finalArgs[:len:len]`) to cap the slice capacity, forcing `append` to allocate a new array\n- Adds a regression test that confirms the args slice is not corrupted during shell completion\n\n## Details\n\nWhen shell completions are requested (e.g., `prog __complete x`), `getCompletions()` calls:\n\n```go\n_ = finalCmd.ParseFlags(append(finalArgs, "--"))\n```\n\n`finalArgs` is a sub-slice of the original args (derived from `os.Args[1:]`), and if it has spare capacity in its backing array, `append` writes `"--"` directly into the shared memory rather than allocating a new slice. This corrupts `os.Args`, which users may be inspecting in their `ValidArgsFunction`.\n\nThe fix uses `finalArgs[:len(finalArgs):len(finalArgs)]` to limit the capacity to the length, guaranteeing that `append` allocates a fresh backing array.\n\nThe bug is most visible with `TraverseChildren: true`, since `Traverse()` returns sub-slices that preserve the original backing array\'s capacity.\n\nFixes #2257\n\n## Test plan\n\n- [x] Added `TestCompletionDoesNotMutateArgs` that fails without the fix and passes with it\n- [x] Full test suite passes (`go test ./...`)', 'author_association': a bare `--` as a flag that "takes a value":\n\n```go\ncase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "--") && !strings.Contains(arg, "="):\n    inFlag = !hasNoOptDefVal(arg[2:], c.Flags())\n    flags = append(flags, The next positional is consumed as that flag\'s "value" and the following positional happens to match a subcommand — so the child handler runs, the first post-`--` positional is silently dropped, and the parent\'s positionals never reach any command.\n\nReproduction from the issue:\n\n```go\nroot := &cobra.Command{Use:"app", TraverseChildren:true, Args:cobra.ArbitraryArgs,\n    Run: func(_ *cobra.Command, args []string){ fmt.Printf("root called with %q\\\\n", args) }}\nroot.AddCommand(&cobra.Command{Use:"child",\n    Run: func(*cobra.Command, []string){ fmt.Println("child called") }})\nroot.Execute()\n```\n\n```\n$ ./app -- literal child\nchild called                 # bug: wrong handler, "literal" lost\n$ # expected:\nroot called with ["literal" "child"]\n```\n\nThe default (non-traverse) `stripFlags` path already stops command discovery on `--`.\n\n## Fix\n\nMirror that behaviour. When `Traverse` sees a bare `--`:\n\n1. Parse any flags accumulated so far on the current command.\n2. 'title': 'fix: stop Traverse command discovery at bare --', 'body': '## Description\n\nFixes #2528.\n\nWith `TraverseChildren: true`, `Command.Traverse` treated a bare `--` as a long flag with an empty name (`arg[2:] == ""`). The next token was consumed as that flag\'s value, then command discovery resumed, so `./app -- literal child` could execute `child` and drop `literal`.\n\n`stripFlags` / `Find` already stop at `--`. Traverse now does the same: when it sees a bare `--` (and is not already collecting a flag value), it returns the current command with the full args for that level so `Execute` parses flags once and keeps later tokens as positionals.\n\n## Checklist\n\n- [x] I have read the [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/spf13/cobra/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).\n- [x] The code has adequate tests for the new feature / bug.\n- [x] Tests pass: `go test -run TestTraverse .`\n\n## Testing\n\n- New: `TestTraverseBareDoubleDashStopsCommandDiscovery` (`-- literal child`, `-- child`, and plain `child` controls).\n- Existing `TestTraverse*` suite passed locally.\n\n## AI assistance\n\nAI tools helped draft the patch, tests, and PR text. I reviewed the change, ran the tests above, and take responsibility for the contents.', 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'ump45nose', 'id': 52391318, 'user_view_type': 'public', 2510, 'state': 'open', 'locked': False, 'title': "Handle combined shorthands in Traverse's value-flag detection", 'body': '## `Traverse` mishandles a combined shorthand cluster that ends in a value flag\n\n### Description\n\n`command.go`, in `Traverse`, the "short flag with a space separated value" case:\n\n```go\ncase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") && len(arg) == 2 && !shortHasNoOptDefVal(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n    inFlag = true\n```\n\n`len(arg) == 2` recognises only a **single** shorthand. A combined cluster such as `-ab` (where `-a` is a bool and `-b` takes a value) is mis-handled: `Traverse` appends `-ab` to `flags` **without** setting `inFlag`, so the following argument is looked up as a **subcommand name**.\n\n### Why it\'s wrong\n\npflag\'s real rule — verified directly with `pflag parse [-ab sub2] err=<nil> args=[] all=true bind="sub2"` — is that the first shorthand lacking a `NoOptDefVal` swallows the rest of the cluster, and only reaches into the next argv slot when it is the *last* shorthand. Cobra must predict that split in order to locate the target command, and for clusters it predicts wrong.\n\nWith `TraverseChildren: true`, `prog child -ab grandchild` fails with:\n\n```\nflag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n```\n\neven though the value *was* supplied — and the equivalent `prog child -a -b grandchild` works. Valid input is rejected with a misleading error.\n\n### Upstream status\n\n- Issue **#2188** ("Combining shorthand flags before command names does not work") is open but is about flags *before* the command name (`mycli -C elephant first second`).\n- PR **#2189** ("Fix shorthand combination edge case") is open and unmerged, and its diff touches only `stripFlags` / `argsMinusFirstX` / `Find` — it does **not** touch `Traverse`, so the `TraverseChildren: true` path is unfixed by any open PR.\n\n## The fix\n\n```go\n// shortCombinationTakesNextArg reports whether the value of a single dash\n// shorthand argument (such as "-a" or "-ab") is taken from the following\n// argument, rather than being embedded in the argument itself.\n//\n// This mirrors how pflag parses shorthand arguments: the first shorthand of the\n// combination that does not have a NoOptDefVal consumes the remainder of the\n// combination as its value, and it only reaches out to the next argument when\n// that shorthand is the last one of the combination. So "-ab value" consumes\n// "value" for -b (when -a is a boolean), while "-bvalue" does not.\nfunc shortCombinationTakesNextArg(combination string, fs *flag.FlagSet) bool {\n\tlast := len(combination) - 1\n\tfor i := 0; i <= last; i++ {\n\t\tif !shortHasNoOptDefVal(combination[i:i+1], fs) {\n\t\t\t// This shorthand needs a value. It only comes from the next argument\n\t\t\t// if the combination ends here.\n\t\t\treturn i == last\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\treturn false\n}\n```\n\nand in `Traverse`:\n\n```diff\n-\t\tcase strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") && len(arg) == 2 && !shortHasNoOptDefVal(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n+\t\tcase len(arg) > 1 && strings.HasPrefix(arg, "-") && !strings.Contains(arg, "=") &&\n+\t\t\tshortCombinationTakesNextArg(arg[1:], c.Flags()):\n```\n\nThe `len(arg) > 1` guard is load-bearing: without it a bare `-` (which pflag treats as a positional argument) would start matching and get appended to `flags`.\n\n## Tests\n\n`TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue` (6 subtests) and `TestExecuteCombinedShorthandWithValue`, both added to `command_test.go`.\n\n- Before:\n  ```\n  --- FAIL: TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue/cluster_ending_in_a_value_flag\n      command_test.go:2501: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n  --- FAIL: TestTraverseCombinedShorthandWithValue/cluster_ending_in_an_inherited_value_flag\n      command_test.go:2501: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'C\' in -C\n  --- FAIL: TestExecuteCombinedShorthandWithValue\n      command_test.go:2543: Unexpected error: flag needs an argument: \'b\' in -b\n  ```\n  After: all pass.\n- Four control subtests (`value_inside_the_cluster`, `all_boolean_cluster`, `single_value_flag`, `single_bool_flag`) pass **both** before and after, proving the fix does not over-consume arguments.\n- `go test ./...`: root package **404 → 412 PASS** (+8), `cobra/doc` 19 PASS, **0 failures**. Baseline on unmodified HEAD was fully green with zero pre-existing failures. `go vet ./...` clean.\n\nThe 36 `gofmt -l` hits are a pre-existing repo-wide CRLF artefact of this Windows checkout — identical count before and after, so this change adds none.\n\n## Note\n\nThis repository asks contributors to sign a CLA; I have not done so, since that is a legal attestation only the contributor can make.\n', 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'januththedev', 'id': 96273863, 'user_view_type': 'public', 'node_id': 'U_kgDOBb0Fxw', 'avatar_url': 'state': 'open', 'locked': False, 'title': 'Provide usefull errors when using invalid sub command', 'body': "If the *TraverseChildren* mode is active, the *Traverse* function returns the last accepted command along the requested sub command chain. This command is then used to parse the arguments. This will for sure fail, if the traversing was aborted because an invalid sub command was given. As a result, cobra complains about invalid flags instead of an invalid sub command.\r\n\r\nThis behaviour might be useful, if the intermediate command is *Runnable()*, but it for sure makes no sense, if it isn't.\r\n\r\nThis PR fixes this by providing a *legacyArgs()* error in case of not runnable intermediate commands.\r\n\r\n---\r\n*Remark:* It solves the obvious problematic behaviour, but basically the general scenario is more complex.\r\nIf the intermediate command is *Runnable()* in addition to providing additional sub commands, then it should be possible to forward the control about the error message to the command to be a able to distinguish between these two cases according to its needs. This is basically already possible by declaring a *FlagErrorFunc()*. But unfortunately it only gets the command and error as arguments, but not the actual set of arguments. Therefore it has no chance to detect the actual problem and provide appropriate error feedback.\r\n\r\nSolving this is more invasive, because it would require, either to change the interface, or add another more general error handler option.\r\n\r\n", 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'mandelsoft', 'id': 553075, 'user_view_type': 'public', 'node_id': 'MDQ6VXNlcjU1MzA3NQ==', 'title': 'fix: treat lone dash as positional during command discovery', 'body': 'When a runnable root command accepts positional arguments and has a `child` subcommand, `root - child` currently executes `child` with `-` as its argument. Replacing `-` with an ordinary filename keeps execution on the root. Enabling `TraverseChildren` also keeps the lone dash on the root, consistent with pflag treating `-` as a positional argument.\n\nUse the existing `isFlagArg` predicate in command discovery and matched-command removal. A lone dash can then stop subcommand discovery like other positional arguments. If an application explicitly defines `-` as a command name or alias, its command token is removed normally. Flag values and the `--` terminator retain their existing handling.\n\nValidation on macOS arm64 with Go 1.25.3:\n\n- The strip-flags case and default-dispatch regressions failed before the fix.\n- Added coverage for lone dashes before and after a subcommand, after a boolean flag, as a flag value, around `--`, and as a command name or alias.\n- `go test ./...` passes.\n- `make all` (formatting and full tests) and `git diff --check` pass. The optional golangci-lint binary is not installed locally.\n\nAI assistance: OpenAI Codex helped implement and test this change.\n', 'author_association': 'NONE', 'user': {'login': 'ibrahimypr', 'state': 'closed', 'locked': False, 'title': 'fix: prevent completions from mutating os.Args via append side effect', 'body': '## Summary\n\n- Fixes a bug where `getCompletions()` accidentally mutates `os.Args` by writing `"--"` into the shared backing array via an `append` with spare capacity\n- Uses a three-index slice expression (`finalArgs[:len:len]`) to cap the slice capacity, forcing `append` to allocate a new array\n- Adds a regression test that confirms the args slice is not corrupted during shell completion\n\n## Details\n\nWhen shell completions are requested (e.g., `prog __complete x`), `getCompletions()` calls:\n\n```go\n_ = finalCmd.ParseFlags(append(finalArgs, "--"))\n```\n\n`finalArgs` is a sub-slice of the original args (derived from `os.Args[1:]`), and if it has spare capacity in its backing array, `append` writes `"--"` directly into the shared memory rather than allocating a new slice. This corrupts `os.Args`, which users may be inspecting in their `ValidArgsFunction`.\n\nThe fix uses `finalArgs[:len(finalArgs):len(finalArgs)]` to limit the capacity to the length, guaranteeing that `append` allocates a fresh backing array.\n\nThe bug is most visible with `TraverseChildren: true`, since `Traverse()` returns sub-slices that preserve the original backing array\'s capacity.\n\nFixes #2257\n\n## Test plan\n\n- [x] Added `TestCompletionDoesNotMutateArgs` that fails without the fix and passes with it\n- [x] Full test suite passes (`go test ./...`)', 'author_association': It includes information about prerequisites, installing the CLI, creating an initial workspace and starter app, and running that app locally to verify your setup.  TRY ANGULAR WITHOUT LOCAL SETUP If you are new to Angular, you might want to start with Try it now!, which introduces the essentials of Angular in the context of a ready-made basic online store app that you can examine and modify. This standalone tutorial takes advantage of the interactive StackBlitz environment for online development. You don't need to set up your local environment until you're ready.  Prerequisites To use the Angular framework, you should be familiar with the following:  JavaScript HTML CSS Knowledge of TypeScript is helpful, but not required.  To install Angular on your local system, you need the following:  Node.js  Angular requires a current, active LTS, or maintenance LTS version of Node.js.  For information about specific version requirements, see the engines key in the package.json file.  For more information on installing Node.js, see nodejs.org. If you are unsure what version of Node.js runs on your system, run node -v in a terminal window.  npm package manager  Angular, the Angular CLI, and Angular applications depend on npm packages for many features and functions. To download and install npm packages, you need an npm package manager. This guide uses the npm client command line interface, which is installed with Node.js by default. To check that you have the npm client installed, run npm -v in a terminal window.  Install the Angular CLI You use the Angular CLI to create projects, generate application and library code, and perform a variety of ongoing development tasks such as testing, bundling, and deployment.  To install the Angular CLI, open a terminal window and run the following command:  content_copy npm install -g @angular/cli Create a workspace and initial application You develop apps in the context of an Angular workspace.  To create a new workspace and initial starter app:  Run the CLI command ng new and provide the name my-app, as shown here:  content_copy ng new my-app The ng new command prompts you for information about features to include in the initial app. Accept the defaults by pressing the Enter or Return key.  The Angular CLI installs the necessary Angular npm packages and other dependencies. This can take a few minutes.  The CLI creates a new workspace and a simple Welcome app, ready to run.  You also have the option to use Angular's strict mode, which can help you write better, more maintainable code. For more information, see Strict mode.  Run the application The Angular CLI includes a server, so that you can build and serve your app locally.  Navigate to the workspace folder, such as my-app.  Run the following command:  content_copy cd my-app ng serve --open The ng serve command launches the server, watches your files, and rebuilds the app as you make changes to those files.  The --open (or just -o) option automatically opens your browser to http://localhost:4200/.  If your installation and setup was successful, you should see a page similar to the following.  Welcome to my-app! Next steps For a more thorough introduction to the fundamental concepts and terminology of Angular single-page app architecture and design principles, read the Angular Concepts section.  Work through the Tour of Heroes Tutorial, a complete hands-on exercise that introduces you to the app development process using the Angular CLI and walks through important subsystems.  To learn more about using the Angular CLI, see the CLI Overview. In addition to creating the initial workspace and app scaffolding, you can use the CLI to generate Angular code such as components and services. The CLI supports the full development cycle, including building, testing, bundling, and deployment.  For more information about the Angular files generated by ng new, see Workspace and Project File Structure.  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------DEPLOYING AN APPLICATION Deploying your application is the process of compiling, or building, your code and hosting the JavaScript, CSS, and HTML on a web server.  This section builds on the previous steps in the Getting Started tutorial and shows you how to deploy your application.  Prerequisites A best practice is to run your project locally before you deploy it. To run your project locally, you need the following installed on your computer:  Node.js.  The Angular CLI. From the terminal, install the Angular CLI globally with:  content_copy npm install -g @angular/cli With the Angular CLI, you can use the command ng to create new workspaces, new projects, serve your application during development, or produce builds to share or distribute.  Running your application locally Download the source code from your StackBlitz project by clicking the Download Project icon in the left menu, across from Project, to download your files.  Create a new Angular CLI workspace using the ng new command, where my-project-name is what you would like to call your project:  content_copy ng new my-project-name This command displays a series of configuration prompts. For this tutorial, accept the default settings for each prompt.  In your newly CLI-generated application, replace the /src folder with the /src folder from your StackBlitz download.  Use the following CLI command to run your application locally:  content_copy ng serve To see your application in the browser, go to http://localhost:4200/. If the default port 4200 is not available, you can specify another port with the port flag as in the following example:  content_copy ng serve --port 4201 While serving your application, you can edit your code and see the changes update automatically in the browser. To stop the ng serve command, press Ctrl+c.  Building and hosting your application To build your application for production, use the build command with the prod flag.  content_copy ng build --prod This command creates a dist folder in the application root directory with all the files that a hosting service needs for serving your application.  If the above ng build command throws an error about missing packages, append the missing dependencies in your local project's package.json file to match the one in the downloaded StackBlitz project.  Copy the contents of the dist/my-project-name folder to your web server. Because these files are static, you can host them on any web server capable of serving files; such as Node.js, Java, .NET, or any backend such as Firebase, Google Cloud, or App Engine. For more information, see Building & Serving and Deployment.  What's next In this tutorial, you've laid the foundation to explore the Angular world in areas such as mobile development, UX/UI development, and server-side rendering. You can go deeper by studying more of Angular's features, engaging with the vibrant community, and exploring the robust ecosystem.  Learning more Angular For a more in-depth tutorial that leads you through building an application locally and exploring many of Angular's most popular features, see Tour of Heroes.  To explore Angular's foundational concepts, see the guides in the Understanding Angular section such as Angular Components Overview or Template syntax. Exploring the Angular ecosystem To support your UX/UI development, see Angular Material.  To test your Angular applications, see Angular Protractor.  The Angular community also has an extensive network of third-party tools and libraries.", 'html_url': 'https://github.com/bikashmaharana16/Ecommproject', 'language': 'TypeScript', 'stargazers_count': 0, 'forks_count': 0, 'open_issues_count': 0, 'updated_at': '2025-05-25T12:01:48Z', 'created_at': '2021-07-03T09:05:19Z', 'private': False, 'fork': False, 'archived': False, 'default_branch': 'main'}, {'id': 382572359, 'name': 'BKecomm', 'full_name': 'bikashmaharana16/BKecomm', 'description': "Project My Project Setting up the local environment and workspace This guide explains how to set up your environment for Angular development using the Angular CLI tool. It includes information about prerequisites, installing the CLI, creating an initial workspace and starter app, and running that app locally to verify your setup.  TRY ANGULAR WITHOUT LOCAL SETUP If you are new to Angular, you might want to start with Try it now!, which introduces the essentials of Angular in the context of a ready-made basic online store app that you can examine and modify. This standalone tutorial takes advantage of the interactive StackBlitz environment for online development. You don't need to set up your local environment until you're ready.  Prerequisites To use the Angular framework, you should be familiar with the following:  JavaScript HTML CSS Knowledge of TypeScript is helpful, but not required.  To install Angular on your local system, you need the following:  Node.js  Angular requires a current, active LTS, or maintenance LTS version of Node.js.  For information about specific version requirements, see the engines key in the package.json file.  For more information on installing Node.js, see nodejs.org. If you are unsure what version of Node.js runs on your system, run node -v in a terminal window.  npm package manager  Angular, the Angular CLI, and Angular applications depend on npm packages for many features and functions. To download and install npm packages, you need an npm package manager. This guide uses the npm client command line interface, which is installed with Node.js by default. To check that you have the npm client installed, run npm -v in a terminal window.  Install the Angular CLI You use the Angular CLI to create projects, generate application and library code, and perform a variety of ongoing development tasks such as testing, bundling, and deployment.  To install the Angular CLI, open a terminal window and run the following command:  content_copy npm install -g @angular/cli Create a workspace and initial application You develop apps in the context of an Angular workspace.  To create a new workspace and initial starter app:  Run the CLI command ng new and provide the name my-app, as shown here:  content_copy ng new my-app The ng new command prompts you for information about features to include in the initial app. Accept the defaults by pressing the Enter or Return key.  The Angular CLI installs the necessary Angular npm packages and other dependencies. This can take a few minutes.  The CLI creates a new workspace and a simple Welcome app, ready to run.  You also have the option to use Angular's strict mode, which can help you write better, more maintainable code. For more information, see Strict mode.  Run the application The Angular CLI includes a server, so that you can build and serve your app locally.  Navigate to the workspace folder, such as my-app.  Run the following command:  content_copy cd my-app ng serve --open The ng serve command launches the server, watches your files, and rebuilds the app as you make changes to those files.  The --open (or just -o) option automatically opens your browser to http://localhost:4200/.  If your installation and setup was successful, you should see a page similar to the following.  Welcome to my-app! Next steps For a more thorough introduction to the fundamental concepts and terminology of Angular single-page app architecture and design principles, read the Angular Concepts section.  Work through the Tour of Heroes Tutorial, a complete hands-on exercise that introduces you to the app development process using the Angular CLI and walks through important subsystems.  To learn more about using the Angular CLI, see the CLI Overview. In addition to creating the initial workspace and app scaffolding, you can use the CLI to generate Angular code such as components and services. The CLI supports the full development cycle, including building, testing, bundling, and deployment.  For more information about the Angular files generated by ng new, see Workspace and Project File Structure.  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------DEPLOYING AN APPLICATION Deploying your application is the process of compiling, or building, your code and hosting the JavaScript, CSS, and HTML on a web server.  This section builds on the previous steps in the Getting Started tutorial and shows you how to deploy your application.  Prerequisites A best practice is to run your project locally before you deploy it. To run your project locally, you need the following installed on your computer:  Node.js.  The Angular CLI. From the terminal, install the Angular CLI globally with:  content_copy npm install -g @angular/cli With the Angular CLI, you can use the command ng to create new workspaces, new projects, serve your application during development, or produce builds to share or distribute.  Running your application locally Download the source code from your StackBlitz project by clicking the Download Project icon in the left menu, across from Project, to download your files.  Create a new Angular CLI workspace using the ng new command, where my-project-name is what you would like to call your project:  content_copy ng new my-project-name This command displays a series of configuration prompts. For this tutorial, accept the default settings for each prompt.  In your newly CLI-generated application, replace the /src folder with the /src folder from your StackBlitz download.  Use the following CLI command to run your application locally:  content_copy ng serve To see your application in the browser, go to http://localhost:4200/. If the default port 4200 is not available, you can specify another port with the port flag as in the following example:  content_copy ng serve --port 4201 While serving your application, you can edit your code and see the changes update automatically in the browser. To stop the ng serve command, press Ctrl+c.  Building and hosting your application To build your application for production, use the build command with the prod flag.  content_copy ng build --prod This command creates a dist folder in the application root directory with all the files that a hosting service needs for serving your application.  If the above ng build command throws an error about missing packages, append the missing dependencies in your local project's package.json file to match the one in the downloaded StackBlitz project.  Copy the contents of the dist/my-project-name folder to your web server. Because these files are static, you can host them on any web server capable of serving files; such as Node.js, Java, .NET, or any backend such as Firebase, Google Cloud, or App Engine. For more information, see Building & Serving and Deployment.  What's next In this tutorial, you've laid the foundation to explore the Angular world in areas such as mobile development, UX/UI development, and server-side rendering. You can go deeper by studying more of Angular's features, engaging with the vibrant community, and exploring the robust ecosystem.  Learning more Angular For a more in-depth tutorial that leads you through building an application locally and exploring many of Angular's most popular features, see Tour of Heroes.  To explore Angular's foundational concepts, see the guides in the Understanding Angular section such as Angular Components Overview or Template syntax.
